questions.explanation: Steel requires specialized fabrication and erection shops; not available in most provinces. Timber CLT requires factory involvement; not locally available. Masonry is possible but inflexible for mixed-use (retail needs long spans; masonry bears walls). RCC frame + CHB infill is ubiquitous in Philippine provinces. Every builder knows the process, local concrete suppliers are common, and skilled masons/carpenters are abundant. Steel requires specialized fabricators and erection crews. Timber and masonry are alternatives, but RCC is the most accessible in limited-labor environments. RCC frame is the go-to system in Philippines due to local expertise. Structural system selection must account for available labor and supply chains.

questions.explanation: Not true; systems differ significantly in MEP integration. CLT can accommodate vertical shafts within panel thickness and at panel joints. Masonry walls make vertical MEP chases difficult due to load bearing requirements. Steel composite decks can incorporate void formers (voids run through the slab), reducing fireproofing and ceiling depth for MEP runs. RCC beams are solid; MEP must run under the structural slab, requiring deeper suspended ceilings. This impacts floor-to-floor and construction cost. Proper MEP planning during structural selection is critical. Structural system affects MEP layout. Engage MEP engineers early. Steel composite decks are most MEP-friendly; RCC requires deeper ceilings; masonry and timber have constraints.
